sources.title: Martin R. Bridson and Andre Haefliger, Metric Spaces of Non-Positive Curvature (Springer Grundlehren 319, 1999; author-hosted PDF)
sources.locator: Chapter I.1, SS1.18-1.20, printed pp. 11-13 (definition of length, arclength function, reparametrization, lower semicontinuity); Chapter I.7, SS7.1-7.13 and SS7.19, printed pp. 97-111 (isometric simplicial complexes, strings and the intrinsic pseudometric, injectivity radius, model simplices, finite-shapes completeness and geodesic existence), with SS7.6, SS7.7, SS7.11 read as the stated pathologies.

contents.name: I.1.18 Definition of length as the supremum of polygonal sums over partitions, and I.1.20(1)-(4) basic length properties (chord bound, invariance under weakly monotone reparametrization, additivity, reversal)
I.1.19 Example: a compact path-connected subspace of the plane with no rectifiable path joining two of its points
contents.reason: A non-rectifiability pathology on a wild planar continuum; this page's items concern rectifiable paths and the chain metric of compact convex cell gluings, and the promised pathology of this pair is the shrinking-edge ray, so no local item consumes I.1.19.

contents.name: I.1.20(5)-(6) continuity of the arclength function and the unique unit-speed arc-length reparametrization of a rectifiable path
I.1.20(7) lower semicontinuity of length under uniform convergence of paths

I.7.2-I.7.4 definition of an M_k-simplicial complex (injectivity and the face-identification/intersection condition), simplices/stars/segments, m-strings and the intrinsic pseudometric as the infimum of string lengths
I.7.5 Lemma: the intrinsic pseudometric and the quotient pseudometric coincide
contents.reason: The page defines the chain metric directly by strings and never introduces the quotient pseudometric of I.5.19, so this identification has no consumer; the local definition takes the string infimum itself as the metric.

contents.name: I.7.6 Remark: the restriction of d to a simplex need not equal the Euclidean metric of that simplex
I.7.7 Example: countably many edges of length 1/n between two vertices make the intrinsic pseudometric degenerate
contents.reason: A degeneration example at a point that is not locally finite; the page proves nondegeneracy under local finiteness and finite shapes, and the pair's promised pathology is the shrinking-edge ray rather than this one.

contents.name: I.7.8-I.7.10 injectivity radius e(x) and the criterion e(x)>0 for the intrinsic pseudometric to be a metric and a length metric
I.7.11 Example: intervals of shrinking length glued end to end give a space isometric to [0,2) with e(x)>0 for all x, so extra hypotheses are needed for completeness
I.7.12-I.7.13 model simplices, characteristic maps, and the theorem that finitely many shapes make (K,d) a complete length space
I.7.14-I.7.16 links of points and cone neighbourhoods in metric simplicial complexes
contents.reason: Angular links and cone neighbourhoods are the spherical-simplex/angular-link page's material; this page needs only the metric topology, and the destination page owns the link metrics consumed later.

contents.name: I.7.17-I.7.18 development of an m-string and radial projection
contents.reason: The taut-string/development machinery is an alternative proof route for I.7.19; this page proves geodesic existence by the proper-target Ascoli argument instead, so no local item consumes developments.

contents.name: I.7.19 Theorem: a connected M_k-simplicial complex with finitely many shapes is a complete geodesic space

sources.title: Michael W. Davis, The Geometry and Topology of Coxeter Groups (first-edition author manuscript, 2007-2008)
sources.locator: Chapter 7, SS7.1-7.3, printed pp. 123-131 (nerve, geometric realizations, Coxeter polytopes and the natural cell structure on Sigma); SS12.1, printed pp. 231-233 (piecewise Euclidean cell structure and the finite-shapes geodesic remark); Appendix I.3, printed pp. 507-508 (X_k-cell structures, the induced length metric, Def. I.3.3, Prop. I.3.4).

contents.name: SS7.1 The nerve L(W,S) of a Coxeter system (Examples 7.1.2-7.1.7)
contents.reason: The spherical-subset nerve is defined on batch26 at def-cg-spherical-nerve-coset-poset-and-davis-realization; its Moussong metric and metric-flag property are defined/proved on batch22. No claim that every Coxeter nerve is combinatorially flag is made by this deferral: the selected claim is metric flag, and the present pair only constructs abstract polyhedral gluings.

contents.name: SS7.2 Geometric realizations: Lemma 7.2.3 (every simplex of Sigma is a translate of a chamber simplex) and Theorem 7.2.4 (the basic construction U(W,K) is W-homeomorphic to Sigma)
contents.reason: The simplicial complex Sigma and the chamber geometry are that page's material; the present page develops the abstract gluing and its intrinsic metric, not the Coxeter-specific realization theorem.

contents.name: SS7.3 Definition 7.3.1 (Coxeter cell = convex hull of a generic orbit), Lemma 7.3.3 (its face poset is W^S for finite W), Proposition 7.3.4 (natural cell structure: cells are Coxeter polytopes glued along faces, 0-skeleton W, 1-skeleton the Cayley graph, 2-skeleton the Cayley 2-complex), Lemma 7.3.5 (Sigma is simply connected)
Examples 7.3.2: the Coxeter cell of C2 is an interval, of the dihedral group D_m is a 2m-gon (regular in the equidistant case), of (C2)^n a cube, of the symmetric group a permutahedron
SS12.1 A piecewise Euclidean cell structure on Sigma (cells C_{W_T}(d_T), edge lengths 2d_s), its length metric, and the remark that finitely many shapes of cells make Sigma a geodesic space
Lemma 12.1.1: the vertex link is a spherical simplex whose cosine matrix is the Coxeter cosine matrix, and SS12.2-12.3 (Moussong's criterion and the CAT(0) theorem)
contents.reason: Link cosines and the CAT(0) theorem are owned by the angular-link, metric-flag and Davis CAT(0) pages; this page stops at the proper complete geodesic metric and does not state curvature.

contents.name: Appendix I.3 Definition I.3.1 (X_k-cell structure on an abstract convex cell complex), the length metric as the infimum of lengths of piecewise geodesic paths, Definition I.3.3 (finitely many shapes) and Proposition I.3.4 (complete geodesic space)
